title: IMAG Teaching Materials
text:
IMAG Teaching Materials
This book accompanies the Cesim Invest simulation (IMAG). You run Asterion Capital, an asset manager with up to four funds, one per client type, invested in 180 assets across five currencies. Each round you read the economic outlook, decide the allocation of every fund in three layers (strategic, tactical, asset level), set fees, and read the results.
This version documents the game flow and how to play it well: what each page of the game asks for, in what order to decide, how to get the numbers with the allocation app that comes with the course, and how to read what comes back. One chapter per step. The theory behind each step (client analysis, capital-market assumptions, mean-variance and Black-Litterman optimization, performance attribution) is referenced where it is used and will be added in a later edition.
How to read it. Chapter 1 shows the whole round on one page. Chapters 2 to 9 follow the order in which you decide. Appendix A is the reference for the allocation app; appendix B collects proposed changes to the app and the game.
The examples. Every worked example in this book uses two invented clients, the Hartley family (home market Britain) and the Keller trust (home market the euro area). They are not clients of the game. The game’s own clients have their own rules, their own risk aversion and their own limits; reading those out of the client cards is your task, and this book shows the method, not the answers.






NoteState of the game



The client descriptions, the guidance bands and the strategic benchmarks described here are the October 2026 design. Until Cesim has loaded them into the simulation, the texts and bands you see on the Clients page may still be the earlier ones. The method does not change.

title: 1  A round in IMAG
text:
1.1 The firm, the funds, the clients
You are a fund manager at Asterion Capital, an asset manager whose founders are stepping back. The firm runs one fund per client type, up to four in total: Conservative, Conservative (ESG), Dynamic and Dynamic (ESG). Each fund has its own clients, its own benchmark and its own fees. The client card on the game’s Clients page tells you the home market, the client’s rules and guidance bands, and the current fee of each fund. You can change the fees every round; the client, the fund type and the client type stay fixed.
Asterion measures everything in US dollars. Assets in other currencies are held unhedged, and the game offers no way to hedge them. The resulting currency risk is part of the risk you manage. The fund’s currency cannot be changed.
The investable universe is 180 assets in four asset classes (government bonds, corporate bonds, equities, alternatives) and five currencies (USD, GBP, EUR, CHF, JPY). Alternatives exist in USD only. A market segment is one asset class in one currency, e.g. “EUR / Corporate bonds”.
Together with the money market, one position per currency, this gives 21 positions in each portfolio (money market, government bonds, corporate bonds and equities in each of the five currencies, plus commodities). The strategic benchmark, the strategic asset allocation (SAA), is defined on the 16 positions without the money market. The optimal portfolio holds no cash: cash is a tactical decision of the player, not a strategic position.

title: 1  A round in IMAG
text:
1.2 What the game measures
Three things drive assets under management (AuM), the money a fund manages:

Risk-adjusted performance against the benchmark. The benchmark of each fund is its strategic allocation. The game’s Analyst page attributes your return against it (currency, asset class, industry, maturity, factors) and compares your strategic allocation with the optimal allocation held in the game’s parameters.
Client satisfaction. Surveys ask whether the fund is managed the way the client expects: inside the limits, with the right amount of risk, with the required sustainability. A fund held far from what the client expects loses clients at once.
Fees. Higher fees turn clients away but raise revenue; clients tolerate fees better when their risk-adjusted return is good. Dynamic clients respond to marketing and accept higher fees; conservative clients want them low and transparent.

AuM drives the firm’s profit, because each fund earns its fee on its AuM. The goal of every fund manager is therefore to grow AuM: deliver good risk-adjusted performance against the benchmark, keep the clients satisfied, and charge appropriate fees.
The instructor picks the winning criterion (Sharpe ratio, alpha, information ratio, cumulative shareholder return of the firm). Whatever it is, it runs through the same three channels.

title: 1  A round in IMAG
text:
1.4 Rounds, practice rounds, teams
A round is typically one quarter. The instructor may run up to three practice rounds before round 1. In a practice round you make decisions and see the results, but nothing carries over; the point is to learn the platform. After the practice rounds the market resets, and round 1 starts from the decisions of the first practice round. Nothing else carries over.
Each team member has a Student Decision Area; the round is scored on the Team Decision Area. Work in your own area, then Copy as team’s decisions; a copy overwrites the team area without backup. Appoint a round CEO who submits, and rotate the role.
Between rounds the game moves your holdings with the market and with fund flows, and, if automation is on, rebalances them to your tactical weights (Chapter 7). The strategic allocation is not touched by this; it is a benchmark, not a holding.

title: 1  A round in IMAG
text:
1.5 The round on one page

Round 1 only: read the client (Ch. 2), read the market (Ch. 3), set and fix the strategic allocation of every fund (Ch. 4), enter it on the Investment strategy page.
Set the ESG floor for the ESG funds in Automation preferences (Ch. 7).
Read the Economic outlook; write down your views with a confidence (Ch. 5).
Run the tactical station for every fund; enter the tactical allocation; check the projected tracking error and information ratio (Ch. 6).
Decide whether to touch asset-level positions; usually not in the first rounds (Ch. 7).
Set fees; read Projections; copy to the team area before the deadline (Ch. 8).
After the deadline: Results and Analyst; revise your γ estimate and your views (Ch. 9).

title: 2  Reading the client
text:
2.1 What the Clients page gives you
In professional investment management, building a portfolio is only one part of the process. Before deciding how to invest, the manager must understand the person the portfolio is being built for. Good investment management starts with the client’s needs.
Each fund has a client card on the Clients page. It shows a general profile of the client type; the Meet client X button introduces a representative client.
The text contains everything the strategic allocation needs. In short, each client has one number and two rules:
Some clients also have a sustainability requirement, and short sales are never allowed. Whatever the card does not mention is not constrained.

title: 2  Reading the client
2  Reading the client
text:
2.2 The rules: read them off
The rules are stated in plain words and mean exactly what they say. “They do not consider commodity futures compatible with their purpose” is a commodity cap of zero; “about five percent in commodities” is a floor of 5 %. “Half of the equities in companies from their home market, the rest spread across the other developed markets in proportion to their size” is the home rule with a home share of one half.
Write the rules down as numbers before you open the app. For the Hartley family, the invented client used throughout this book, the rules read:

Home market Britain. Commodities at least 5 %. Half of the equity book in UK companies, the rest by market size. No sustainability requirement. Cash at the manager’s discretion.

title: 2  Reading the client
section: 2.3 The risk aversion: bracket it from two decisions
text:
2.3 The risk aversion: bracket it from two decisions
The client card describes decisions the client has taken in the past. Each is a choice between two portfolios. For each portfolio the card gives two numbers: its volatility \(\sigma\) and its expected return over cash \(\mu\).
We need to turn those two decisions into a number, the client’s risk aversion \(\gamma\). The idea is simple. A risk-averse client dislikes volatility. Offered a portfolio with more return and more volatility and one with less of both, the client’s choice tells us roughly how much they dislike volatility. Two decisions give us two constraints, one on each side of the true \(\gamma\), and together they bracket it.

2.3.1 The utility function, in one line
To make “how much they dislike volatility” precise, we assume the client values a portfolio by its mean–variance utility:
\[
U = \mu - \frac{\gamma}{2}\sigma^2
\]
Read it as: utility = return minus a penalty for risk. The penalty is \(\frac{\gamma}{2}\) times the variance, so a client with a higher \(\gamma\) penalises risk more heavily. This is the standard Markowitz utility function, and the \(\gamma\) in it is the same risk aversion that appears in mean–variance optimisation in Chapter 4. Higher \(\gamma\) means a more cautious client.
A client prefers portfolio A to portfolio B when \(U_A > U_B\). Every past decision on the card is a statement of that form, and each one can be solved for \(\gamma\).


2.3.2 What one decision tells us
Take one decision. The client chose one portfolio over another. Call the one they chose the winner and the other the loser. We do not yet need to know which is riskier; write the winner’s return and volatility as \(\mu_W, \sigma_W\) and the loser’s as \(\mu_L, \sigma_L\).
The client preferred the winner, so its utility must be higher:
\[
\mu_W - \frac{\gamma}{2}\sigma_W^2 > \mu_L - \frac{\gamma}{2}\sigma_L^2
\]
Move the \(\gamma\) terms to the left and the return terms to the right:
\[
\frac{\gamma}{2}\left(\sigma_L^2 - \sigma_W^2\right) > \mu_L - \mu_W
\]
Now look at the sign of \(\sigma_L^2 - \sigma_W^2\). It is positive if the loser was the riskier portfolio and negative if the winner was. That sign decides which way the inequality points, and therefore whether the decision gives us a floor or a ceiling on \(\gamma\).
Case 1: the client turned down the riskier portfolio. The winner is the quieter one, so the loser had the larger variance and \(\sigma_L^2 - \sigma_W^2 > 0\). Dividing by a positive number keeps the inequality pointing the same way:
\[
\gamma > \frac{2(\mu_L - \mu_W)}{\sigma_L^2 - \sigma_W^2}
\]
The client gave up some return to get a quieter portfolio. That means they must be at least this risk-averse. The decision gives us a floor on \(\gamma\).
Case 2: the client took the riskier portfolio. The winner is the riskier one, so the loser had the smaller variance and \(\sigma_L^2 - \sigma_W^2 < 0\). Dividing by a negative number flips the inequality:
\[
\gamma < \frac{2(\mu_W - \mu_L)}{\sigma_W^2 - \sigma_L^2}
\]
The client was willing to accept more swing to get more return. That means they cannot be more risk-averse than this. The decision gives us a ceiling on \(\gamma\).


2.3.3 The one formula to remember
Notice that the right-hand side is the same expression in both cases, once you put the riskier portfolio on top. Write \(X\) for the riskier portfolio and \(Y\) for the quieter one. Then:
\[
\text{bound} = \frac{2(\mu_X - \mu_Y)}{\sigma_X^2 - \sigma_Y^2}
\]
and the only question is whether it is a floor or a ceiling:

If the client rejected the riskier portfolio \(X\), the bound is a floor: \(\gamma > \text{bound}\).
If the client chose the riskier portfolio \(X\), the bound is a ceiling: \(\gamma < \text{bound}\).

That is the whole method. You do not need to remember two formulas. You need to remember one expression and one question: which portfolio did the client end up with? If they ended up with the quieter one, the expression is a floor. If they ended up with the riskier one, it is a ceiling.


2.3.4 Two conditions for the bound to mean anything
The method only works if the two portfolios are genuinely different in both dimensions.

The riskier portfolio must also offer more return. If the riskier portfolio offered less return, no sensible client would hold it, and the choice would tell us nothing about \(\gamma\). Always check that \(\mu_X > \mu_Y\) before applying the formula.
Both numbers must be in the same units. Put \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) in the same units (both decimals, both annualised). The \(\gamma\) you recover is then on the same scale as the \(\gamma\) that goes into the mean–variance optimiser in Chapter 4.

If either condition fails, the decision is not usable and you should look for another one on the card.


2.3.5 Worked example: the Hartleys
Decision 1: they turned down the riskier portfolio. With their previous adviser they rejected a portfolio with 10 % volatility and 6.9 % expected return over cash, and took one with 8 % volatility and 5.9 % instead. Here \(X=(10\%,\,6.9\%),\ Y=(8\%,\,5.9\%)\), and because they rejected \(X\) this is a lower bound:
\[
\gamma > \frac{2(0.069-0.059)}{0.10^2-0.08^2}=\frac{0.020}{0.0036}=5.6
\]
Decision 2: they kept the riskier portfolio. Later, offered an alternative with 6 % volatility and 5.1 % expected return over cash, they stayed with their portfolio of 8 % volatility and 6.6 %. Here \(X=(8\%,\,6.6\%),\ Y=(6\%,\,5.1\%)\), and because they chose \(X\) this is an upper bound:
\[
\gamma < \frac{2(0.066-0.051)}{0.08^2-0.06^2}=\frac{0.030}{0.0028}=10.7
\]
So the two decisions bracket the Hartleys:
\[
5.6 < \gamma < 10.7
\]
that is, \(\gamma\) lies between about 5.5 and 11.
Placing \(\gamma\) inside the bracket. The bracket comes from what the client did; the words on the card place \(\gamma\) within it:

“Lived through two bear markets without selling, but would not want to see a year like 2008 again” → middle of the bracket.
“They need the portfolio to grow; income covers spending” → lower end (growth first, more tolerant of risk).
“The income the portfolio produces matters more than growth” → higher end (capital preservation, less tolerant of risk).

For the Hartleys the bear-market comment points to the middle, so we take \(\gamma=8\).

title: 2  Reading the client
text:
2.4 From γ to a portfolio
Once \(\gamma\) is estimated, it does two things in the rest of the book. It selects the strategic allocation in Chapter 4, and it sets the prior of the Black–Litterman step in Chapters 5 and 6.
In Chapter 4, the client’s \(\gamma\) selects the point on the efficient frontier that maximises \(U=\mu-\frac{\gamma}{2}\sigma^2\). A higher \(\gamma\) selects a portfolio with less variance and a lower expected return; a lower \(\gamma\) selects a riskier one with a higher expected return. Do not read γ off a conventional profile table (“above 6 is conservative”): which equity share a γ produces depends on the data and the client’s rules. The Hartleys, at γ = 8, hold 46.5 % equities; the check is the guidance bands below, not a rule of thumb.






Warningγ is the whole game at this step



The rules are the same for every reader of the card. What distinguishes a careful reading from a careless one is the estimate of \(\gamma\). Chapter 4 shows what it costs to be wrong: for the Hartleys, \(\gamma = 7\) or \(9\) instead of \(8\) puts the allocation 7 or 5.5 points away from the benchmark; the ends of the bracket cost 14 to 23 points.

title: 2  Reading the client
text:
2.5 The guidance bands
Guidance bands are quoted in the text (“between 15 and 52 percent in government bonds”). They are the range inside which the client expects to be held, and they are consistent with the client’s risk aversion: every γ in the bracket gives an allocation inside the bands, and a γ outside the bracket leaves at least one band. Use them two ways: as a check on your allocation, and to narrow the bracket. If your allocation leaves a band, your γ is outside the bracket.
A fund held far from what the card describes loses the client, whatever the market does; a dynamic client parked in money market walks away. Lost clients mean lower AuM and lower profit, and in the end put the firm in financial difficulty.

title: 2  Reading the client
text:
2.6 The home market
Meet client X names the home market. It decides which equity market carries the home share of the equity book; the rest of the book goes to the other markets by capitalization (US 70.0, euro area 14.5, Japan 5.9, Switzerland 5.7, Britain 4.0 percent of the universe, renormalized without the home market). Because the home rule puts a large part of the equities into a market the data might not otherwise hold at that size, the rest of the allocation adjusts around it: two clients with the same γ and different home markets do not hold the same class mix. That is the method working, not a mistake.

2.6.1 Why the rest goes by size
The home share is the client’s own choice: most investors hold more of their home market than its size alone would justify, the well-documented home bias (French and Poterba 1991). For the rest of the equity book the client states no view, and the allocation should not invent one. Market capitalization is the weighting that needs no forecast. It is the market portfolio of the CAPM (Sharpe 1964), the one portfolio all investors can hold together, so any other weighting is a bet against the average investor (Sharpe 1991). It also protects the allocation from the optimizer: the expected returns of the five equity markets are estimated with an error larger than the differences between them, and a free optimization turns that noise into extreme weights, often a whole market at zero (Michaud 1989). Fixing the regional split by size leaves γ as the one number the reading of the card has to get right. And it keeps the strategic allocation consistent with Chapters 5 and 6, which reverse-optimize it into the prior of the Black–Litterman step: with the regions at market weights, that prior is close to the market equilibrium Black and Litterman start from (Black and Litterman 1992). The price of the rule is concentration. The United States is 70 percent of the universe, and capitalization weights follow a market into its bubbles, as Japan’s share of world equity around 1989 showed.

title: 2  Reading the client
text:
2.7 Sustainability
A client who requires a minimum rating holds only securities that pass it. This binds when tactical weights become positions (Chapter 7), not at the strategic level: the class-level statistics of the market do not change with the filter.

title: 3  Reading the market
text:
3.1 Two sources of information, two uses
Once you know the client, the next step is the market you invest in, because the strategic allocation is built on it. Asset classes differ: some are more volatile than others, some have a higher expected return, some move together and others in opposite directions.
The game gives you two different things about the market, and they serve two different decisions.
Keep the two apart. The benchmark does not move with the outlook.

title: 3  Reading the market
text:
The history. The course dataset (loaded in the allocation app) holds the full history of the 21 positions: monthly total returns in US dollars, unhedged, and the US money-market rate. The strategic allocation of every client is defined on this history (Chapter 4). The game’s own Results page also lets you download the last five years of asset, factor and exchange-rate data as an Excel file; that is a subset of the same market.
The Economic outlook. Each round, the analyst estimates the coming period: interest rates by maturity and currency, inflation and growth, factor premia, with an expected range around every estimate. This is forward-looking information and belongs to the tactical decision (Chapter 5). It is not an input to the strategic allocation.

title: 3  Reading the market
section: 3.2 Station 1 of the app: statistics and correlations
text:
3.2 Station 1 of the app: statistics and correlations
Open the app (https://inno.uni.li/apps/invest/), station 1 · Strategic Asset Analysis. Keep the default selection (the 16 benchmark positions; the five money-market positions can be added for analysis) and the sample at the full history. The statistics table is annualised and in excess of the US money-market rate; the correlation matrix is of the same excess returns.
Three things to take from the table before you optimise anything.
The ranking by Sharpe ratio. Sort the table by the Sharpe column and read it top to bottom. The equity markets and the US bond positions sit at the top; the positions in a foreign currency other than equities sit at the bottom, several of them with a Sharpe ratio around zero or below. Ask of every position near the bottom what premium it is being paid.
What a foreign bond is in dollars. Compare the volatility of a country’s money-market position with that of its government bonds, and look at the correlation between the two. In dollars both are mostly the currency: the money market has the currency’s volatility on an excess return near zero, and the bond adds a few points of premium on top of the same currency risk. The game cannot hedge. Keep this in mind when you read the optimiser’s output in Chapter 4, and when you consider a tactical position in Chapter 6.
The correlation structure. The five equity markets move together, with correlations around 0.4 to 0.65 against the US; US government bonds are slightly negatively correlated with US equities. That negative correlation is what a defensive position is for.






NoteWhere the money market is



Excess returns are measured over the US money-market rate, so the money market is the zero line of the table. The five money-market positions themselves are not in the benchmark: the game’s strategic grid has no cash row, and the client leaves cash to the manager. Add them in station 1 if you want to see them (in dollars, a foreign money-market position is the currency and nothing else); leave them out when you optimise the strategic allocation.

title: 3  Reading the market
text:
3.3 What not to do here

Do not shift means or volatilities “to reflect your view”. The strategic benchmark is the sample; views enter in Chapter 5.
Do not shorten the sample for the strategic allocation. The client’s benchmark is defined on the full history; a shorter window produces a different allocation and a worse score.
Do not drop benchmark positions from the selection. Zero weights are the optimiser’s job, and the statistics of the full benchmark universe are what the attribution later refers to.

title: 3  Reading the market
text:
3.4 Deliverable of this step
Nothing to type into the game. What you should be able to say: which positions carry a portfolio and why; what a foreign bond or money-market position is, seen from the dollar; what the correlation between equities and US government bonds buys you.

title: 4  Setting the strategic allocation
text:
4.1 What the optimiser is doing
With the client and the market understood, the next step is the strategic allocation, the benchmark against which every tactical decision is measured. The strategic allocation is entered once per fund on the Investment strategy page and stays for the whole game. It is the benchmark: risk-adjusted performance, attribution and the strategic allocation analysis on the Analyst page are measured against it. The game also holds, invisibly, the allocation its parameters say is optimal for the client; the closer your strategic allocation is to it, the better the client is served.
That optimal allocation is not arbitrary: it follows a fixed rule, and this book states the rule. It is the solution to a quadratic optimisation problem:
So the task is not to invent an allocation. It is to estimate γ well (Chapter 2) and run the optimisation on the right data.
The objective above is mean–variance optimisation (MVO), the framework introduced by Markowitz (1952). It is worth a moment on what it does, because the output only makes sense if you know what the optimiser is trying to achieve.
Every candidate portfolio has two summary numbers. Its expected excess return is the weighted average of the excess returns of its holdings. Its variance is not just the weighted average of the holdings’ variances: it also depends on how the holdings move together (their covariances). Two assets that move in lockstep diversify nothing; two that move independently partly offset each other. That is the whole point of diversification, and it is the reason the optimiser does not simply pile into the single highest-return asset.
Plot every possible portfolio in (volatility, expected return) space and you get a cloud. The upper-left edge of that cloud is the efficient frontier: the portfolios that offer the most expected return for their level of risk. Any portfolio below the frontier is dominated: another portfolio offers more return for the same risk, or less risk for the same return. The optimiser finds the frontier and then picks the one point on it that the client’s \(\gamma\) selects. A higher \(\gamma\) pushes the choice down and to the left (quieter, lower return); a lower \(\gamma\) pushes it up and to the right (riskier, higher return).
Two consequences follow, and both matter for the checks:

title: 4  Setting the strategic allocation
text:
Figure 4.1: The Markowitz Efficient Frontier





The allocation is a point on the frontier, not a forecast. It says “given these inputs and this \(\gamma\), this is the best trade-off available.” It does not say which asset class will win next year.
MVO is sensitive to its inputs. Small changes in expected returns or in the covariance matrix can move the optimal weights a long way, sometimes into concentrated positions. That is why the checks below look not only at the weights but at what the optimiser chose to leave at zero.

title: 4  Setting the strategic allocation
section: 4.4 The checks before you fix it
text:
4.4 The checks before you fix it

The rules are met and nothing else binds. The station lists the binding limits; for a well-read client only the floor you entered appears.
Inside the guidance bands. For the Hartleys the card quotes government bonds 15–52 %, corporate bonds 6–18 %, equities 37–63 %. The example sits inside all three. If a class is outside its band, your γ is outside the bracket: move it toward the middle.
Home share of the equity book as stated. Rounding moves it by a point.
Plausible risk. Worst year and drawdown should fit the words on the card. The Hartleys “would not want to see a year like 2008 again”; a worst year of −14 % in thirty years is consistent with that, a worst year of −23 % is not.
Look at what is zero. If a position with a Sharpe ratio near zero in station 1 appears in the allocation, a limit is forcing it. Ask which.

section: 5.2 Reading the outlook: the business cycle
text:
5.2 Reading the outlook: the business cycle
The outlook gives you numbers. Your job is not to copy them into the app; it is to decide whether you believe them, and where you disagree. The Investment Clock is the lens that turns the outlook’s economic indicators into a view about which asset classes are likely to lead and lag over the coming quarters.

5.2.1 The cycle in one paragraph
Economic variables do not move independently. Growth, inflation, employment and confidence evolve together through a recurring pattern of expansion and contraction. The pattern is not a law, but it is a useful empirical regularity. The framework classifies the economy by two things: the direction of growth relative to trend (rising or falling) and the direction of inflation (rising or falling). Those two directions define four phases. Each phase has historically favoured a different asset class, and the outlook’s numbers are what tell you which phase the economy is in.
The framework is the Investment Clock of Greetham and Hartnett (2004). The four phases and the asset-class rotation they imply are summarised in the figure below.

The outlook reports, for each economy, the GDP path, the inflation path, the unemployment rate and confidence indices. The classification combines the direction of growth with the direction of inflation.

5.2.4 Cross-checks
The classification is a hypothesis, not a conclusion. The outlook supplies two further sources of evidence that can confirm or contradict it.
Sector data. The four phases favour different equity sectors. Cyclical and value sectors (industrials, basic materials) lead in Overheat and Recovery; defensive growth sectors (consumer staples) lead in Reflation; defensive value sectors (oil and gas, pharmaceuticals, utilities) lead in Stagflation. If the sector table shows cyclical and value sectors leading over the recent windows, that is consistent with an Overheat or Recovery classification. If it shows defensive growth leading, that is inconsistent, and you should lower your confidence in the classification or reconsider it.
Factor data. The outlook supplies value (HML), momentum (MOM) and robustness (RMW) premia per currency. Falling inflation favours growth stocks; rising inflation favours value stocks. Momentum is not tied to the level of growth or inflation but to the persistence of the market’s direction: a clear phase transition favours momentum, a stalled or backward clock does not. If the factor data shows momentum leading, that is consistent with a market moving through a phase transition. If value is weakening while the classification says inflation is rising, that is a counter-signal.
The rule is simple: two or more confirming signals support the classification; a confirming signal and a contradicting one lower your confidence; a classification contradicted by both the sector and factor data should be revisited before you enter a view. The confidence you set in the Black–Litterman step (below) should reflect how many signals agree.


5.2.5 What the classification gives you
A direction for each segment, and a confidence based on the cross-checks. That is the input to the Black–Litterman step. The classification does not tell you how much to tilt; the Black–Litterman model does that, weighted by your confidence and by the size of the gap between the outlook and the prior.

text:
5.3 A view, in the form the app needs
Station 3 of the app takes views in the Black–Litterman form; station 4 turns them into tilts away from the strategic allocation. Each view is either:

Absolute: “position A earns x percent a year over cash”. Example: US equities earn 12 %.
Relative: “position A beats position B by x points a year”. Example: euro-area equities beat Swiss equities by 2 points.

Each view has a confidence between 5 and 95 percent. The prior the views are measured against is not the sample mean but the equilibrium implied by the fixed SAA: the expected returns under which the client’s strategic allocation is exactly optimal (Π = γΣw). With no views the posterior equals the prior, and the tactical allocation (Chapter 6) equals the strategic one. A view that agrees with the prior leaves it there too. Every deviation you see later can be traced to a view you entered.

title: 5  From the Economic outlook to views
text:
5.4 Turning the outlook into views
A practical recipe, per round:

Start from the prior table in station 3 (column “Prior, implied by the SAA”). For the Hartleys’ SAA the implied excess return of US equities is 7.5 %, of UK equities 9.5 %, of US government bonds 0.4 %.
Compare with the outlook. Build the outlook’s expected excess return for a segment the way the game does: for equities, the expected excess market return plus the factor premia you expect the segment to earn (the analyst’s figures, or your own); for government bonds, the change in yields you expect (a rise in yields is a negative return for a constant-maturity bond: roughly minus duration times the yield change) plus the running yield; for corporate bonds the same plus the spread.
State the difference as a view, in annual terms. If the outlook says US equities should do better than the prior implies, enter an absolute view above 7.5 %. If it says only that one market beats another, enter a relative view; relative views are safer, because they do not require you to translate a quarterly estimate into an annual level.
Set the confidence from the expected range. An estimate at the centre of a narrow range: 70 to 80 %. An estimate at the edge of its range, or a narrative you half believe: 30 to 50 %. The default 50 % is the textbook He–Litterman setting.
Keep τ at 0.05 unless you want every view to move the allocation more (higher τ) or less (lower τ).
Read the posterior table: which positions moved, by how much, and whether the sign is the one you meant. The “Change” column is your view after the model has weighed it against the prior.







TipOne set of views for all funds



Views are about the market, not about the client. Enter the same views for every fund; the tilt they produce differs by client (Chapter 6), because each fund has its own prior and its own γ. The app keeps the views and lets you switch the fixed SAA it is applied to.

Outlook: the analyst’s expected excess market return for USD is at the top of its range, the US narrative is strong, and the factor premia are positive. We hold the view that US equities earn 12 % over cash next year, confidence 50 %, τ = 0.05.

Do not enter the sample mean as a view. It is already in the SAA.

title: 6  Setting the tactical allocation
text:
6.1 What the model does
By default the game copies the strategic allocation into the tactical allocation. Disabling the automatic tactical allocation on the Investment strategy page opens the tactical grid. There you use your views to tilt the tactical allocation away from the strategic one. The tactical allocation is the one the round is run on; the strategic allocation stays the benchmark. The page estimates the tracking error of your tactical allocation against the benchmark and the projected information ratio from the forecast returns.
The tactical step is a Black–Litterman model. It takes the strategic allocation as the starting point, blends in the views you entered in station 3, and produces a posterior set of expected returns. Station 4 then optimises the tactical allocation on those posterior returns, within the band and the tracking-error budget. The point of the model is that the tilt is driven by your views and not by the optimiser chasing noise in the expected-return estimates.

title: 6  Setting the tactical allocation
text:
6.1.1 The prior: the strategic allocation, reverse-optimised
The model starts from the strategic allocation. Rather than asking “what returns do I expect?”, it asks the reverse question: what expected returns would make the strategic allocation optimal? That is the prior, and it is the same one introduced in the previous chapter:
\[
\Pi = \gamma \Sigma w
\]
where \(w\) is the strategic allocation, \(\Sigma\) is the covariance matrix, and \(\gamma\) is the client’s risk aversion. The prior encodes both the capital market assumptions and the client’s risk tolerance. If you have no views, the posterior equals the prior, and the tactical allocation equals the strategic one.


6.1.2 The views
A view is a statement about expected returns, expressed in one of two forms:

Absolute: “US equities earn 12 % over cash”. In the model this is a row of the view matrix \(P\) that picks out US equities, with the view’s expected return in the corresponding row of \(Q\).
Relative: “euro-area equities beat Swiss equities by 2 points”. This is a row of \(P\) with \(+1\) on euro-area equities and \(-1\) on Swiss equities, and the 2 points in \(Q\). A relative view does not move both positions the same way: it moves the long side up and the short side down, in proportion to how precise the view is.

Each view has a confidence, which enters the model through the matrix \(\Omega\). A high-confidence view has a small entry in \(\Omega\) (low uncertainty); a low-confidence view has a large entry. In station 3 the views are treated as independent, so \(\Omega\) is diagonal and each view’s confidence affects only that view’s pull on the posterior.


6.1.3 The posterior
The posterior expected returns are the precision-weighted average of the prior and the views:
\[
E(R) = \underbrace{\left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} + P^T\Omega^{-1}P\right]^{-1}}_{\text{combined precision}}
       \underbrace{\left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1}\Pi + P^T\Omega^{-1}Q\right]}_{\text{precision-weighted sum}}
\]
Every symbol is one of four things: an input you supply, a parameter you set, a matrix the station builds from your views, or a quantity the model computes. The table lists them all.








Symbol
What it is
In the station




\(E(R)\)
The posterior expected excess returns, one per position.
The output. These are the returns station 4 optimises on.


\(\Pi\)
The prior expected excess returns, one per position.
Computed from the fixed SAA: \(\Pi = \gamma\Sigma w\).


\(\Sigma\)
The covariance matrix of the positions.
From station 2’s sample covariance.


\(\tau\)
A scalar that scales the uncertainty in the prior.
An input. Default 0.05.


\(P\)
The view matrix. Each row is one view: \(+1\) on the position the view is “for”, \(-1\) on the position it is “against” (or a single \(+1\) for an absolute view).
Built by the station from the views you entered.


\(Q\)
The view returns, one per view: the expected return the view asserts, in annual terms.
Built by the station from the views you entered.


\(\Omega\)
The view covariance matrix, diagonal when views are independent. Each diagonal entry is the variance of the corresponding view.
Built by the station from the confidence you set on each view.


\((\tau\Sigma)^{-1}\)
The precision of the prior: how strongly the model believes the strategic allocation.
Computed.


\(P^T\Omega^{-1}P\)
The precision of the views: how strongly the model believes your views, in the directions they point.
Computed.



With the symbols in hand, the formula says one thing: the posterior is a weighted average of the prior \(\Pi\) and the views \(Q\), with the weights set by their relative precision. If the views are very precise relative to the prior, the posterior is pulled close to \(Q\). If the prior is very precise, the posterior stays close to \(\Pi\). If there are no views, \(P\) and \(Q\) are empty, \(P^T\Omega^{-1}P = 0\), and the posterior equals the prior.
What \(\tau\) and \(\Omega\) do. \(\tau\) scales the uncertainty in the prior. A larger \(\tau\) means the model is less confident in the strategic allocation, so the views receive relatively more weight; a smaller \(\tau\) anchors the posterior more firmly to the strategic allocation. The conventional choice, and the default in station 3, is \(\tau = 0.05\). Changing \(\tau\) changes every view’s influence at once; it is not a per-view setting. \(\Omega\) encodes the confidence in each view. A smaller entry means the model treats the view as more precise, so the posterior moves further; a larger entry means the view is treated as noisy, so the posterior moves less. Together, \(\tau\) and \(\Omega\) determine how far the tactical allocation tilts away from the strategic one.


6.1.4 Why the tactical step differs from the strategic one
The Black–Litterman posterior is used in station 4 with three modifications relative to station 2:

No home rule. The home rule defines the benchmark, so keeping it in the tactical step would force the equity book to grow or shrink in fixed regional proportions, and a view on one market could not act. The client’s other limits stay, the commodity floor included.
The sample covariance. Risk is measured with the covariance of station 2, not the posterior covariance. Using the posterior covariance would raise measured risk as soon as any view is entered, and push every fund from equities into bonds regardless of what the view said.
Band and tracking-error budget. The maximum deviation per position (default ± 5 points) and the tracking-error budget (default 2 % a year) limit how far the tactical allocation can stray from the benchmark. If the optimum exceeds the budget, the deviation is scaled down to it.

With these in place, every deviation from the strategic allocation is traceable to a view. A view that agrees with the prior leaves the tactical allocation at the strategic one; a view that disagrees produces a tilt, and the size of the tilt is set by the confidence and by the band and budget.

title: 6  Setting the tactical allocation
text:
6.4 Two cautions
An absolute view on a foreign-currency position is also a currency view. The game’s data are in dollars, unhedged, and all positions in one currency share that currency. Take the view “euro-area government bonds earn 4 % over cash”, confidence 50 %. For the Hartleys the station moves 5 points into euro-area government bonds and 5 more into euro-area corporate bonds, on which you had no view, funded from US bonds. That is 10 points of euro against the dollar; tracking error 1.0 %. For a view on foreign rates, state it relative to US government bonds: “euro-area government bonds beat US government bonds by 3.5 points” (the prior spread is 1.8). That says what the bet is. It does not remove the euro: here the station builds the same 10-point euro position. Read the currency totals of the deviation matrix before you enter it.
The client’s commodity floor stays a floor. A negative view cannot take commodities below it. Give the Hartleys the view “commodities earn 0 % over cash” (prior 2.6 %): commodities stay at 5 %, and the station rearranges the rest instead, government bonds +4 points, corporate bonds −3.5, equities −0.5. The expected active return is −0.1 %, and the app flags it: the tilt buys lower risk, not return. If the floor blocks your view, leave the fund at its SAA.

title: 6  Setting the tactical allocation
text:
6.5 Entering it in the game

Investment strategy → disable Automatic tactical allocation for the fund.
Type the tactical matrix (currency × asset class) from station 4.
Read the game’s tracking-error estimate and projected information ratio. The estimate will not equal the app’s exactly (the game uses its own forecast returns and a shorter history), but the order of magnitude must agree. A projected information ratio below zero means the game’s forecasts disagree with your views; decide which you believe.
Repeat for every fund with the same views.

title: 6  Setting the tactical allocation
text:
6.6 Rules of thumb

Tracking error 1 to 3 % a year is a normal tactical budget for a fund with a fixed benchmark; conservative clients at the low end.
A tilt into a foreign bond is a currency bet. The attribution will show it as a currency effect. Make it only if it is the bet you mean. Cash is outside the benchmark: parking part of the fund in money market is an under-investment against every class, and the information ratio will say so.
A negative expected active return is a warning. Use fewer views, relative rather than absolute, or a narrower band, or leave the fund at its SAA.
Stay close to what the card describes. The band in station 4 is your choice, not a client limit, and the tactical step does not impose the home rule. A tactical matrix far from the guidance bands costs clients.
Re-enter every round. Between rounds the game moves holdings with returns and flows; the tactical grid you entered last round is not where the fund is now.
No views, no tilt. If the outlook gives you nothing you believe, leave the automatic tactical allocation on. Zero tracking error is a decision, not a failure.

title: 7  From tactical weights to positions
text:
7.1 Automation preferences: the ESG floor
The tactical asset allocation is a grid of segment weights. The game’s automatic allocation translates each segment weight into positions, by value weighting or equal weighting, and rebalances them to the tactical weights after each round unless you switch it off.
For the first rounds, leave this automation on. The decisions that matter are above it.
Automatic and benchmark portfolio preferences is where the ESG requirement of the ESG funds is set: Minimum criteria → ESG rating → A (or the numeric threshold the game uses for A). The filter removes every asset below the floor from the fund’s investable set, in the current allocation and in the benchmark portfolio.
Two things to check:
crumbs: 7  From tactical weights to positions

title: 7  From tactical weights to positions
text:
The Matches column. A warning sign means a segment has no asset that passes the filter; money allocated to that segment stays in cash. On this universe an A floor should pass in every equity segment; if it does not, lower the threshold one notch rather than leave cash.
The weighting. Value weighting for equities is the default and matches the way the strategic allocation split the equity book across markets by capitalisation. Keep it.







NoteWhy ESG binds here and not earlier



Ratings exist for equities only, and the market carries no ESG premium: the class-level statistics of station 1 are unchanged by the filter. What the filter costs is diversification inside each equity segment, which shows up as tracking error of the fund’s stock book against the segment line, not as a different strategic allocation. That is why the ESG funds’ strategic allocations differ from the others only by “no commodities” and by γ.
crumbs: 7  From tactical weights to positions

title: 7  From tactical weights to positions
text:
7.2 Asset-level decisions (optional)
Disabling Automatic current allocation opens the Markets page for asset-level decisions: the list of 180 assets with performance, benchmark weight, factor loadings, industry, maturity; each asset’s page with description, history, metrics and fundamentals. The Economic outlook’s Instrument performance subpage lets you enter an asset-level alpha if you expect a single asset to beat its segment.
Our advice: do not do it in the practice rounds or in round 1. Security selection on top of the tactical tilt adds a layer of tracking error that is hard to attribute later, and the automation already produces a sensible, diversified book. If you do it:

Keep the segment totals equal to the tactical weights, or the tactical decision is overwritten by the asset-level one.
Prefer deviations inside a segment (overweight one issuer, underweight another) to deviations across segments.
Write down the thesis per deviation; the Analyst page attributes by industry, maturity and factor, and you will want to recognise your own bets.
crumbs: 7  From tactical weights to positions

title: 7  From tactical weights to positions
text:
7.3 Analyzing the fundamentals
If you decide to deviate from the automatic weight of a single asset, you need a thesis. A thesis is not “the stock is cheap” or “it has done well recently.” A thesis is a statement about the company’s fundamentals that the market has not yet priced in. The asset page provides the fundamentals you need to form one.
You do not need to be an accountant. You need to look at three things: whether the earnings are real (quality of earnings), how safely the company is financed (solvency and liquidity), and whether the price already reflects the good news (relative valuation).

7.3.1 What the page gives you
Before running the analysis, it helps to know what data the game provides. The asset page contains much more than the ratios we cover here. The available fields are:

Asset information: Asset class, area, country, industry, home currency.
Performance metrics: Price, return over 3 months, 1 year and 5 years, market capitalization.
Factor loadings: Alpha, market beta, HML beta, MOM beta, RMW beta (both for the last round and long-term).
Other metrics: Sharpe ratio.
Fundamentals overview (up to five years): Earnings per share (EPS), price-to-earnings (P/E), return on equity (ROE), return on investment (ROI), debt-to-equity, dividend yield, free cash flow (FCF) per share, revenue, operating margin, current ratio.
ESG ratings (up to five years): Environmental, Social, Governance, and Overall scores.

The analysis below focuses on the three important checks for security selection: Quality of Earnings, Solvency and Liquidity, and Relative Valuation. Other common ratios, such as price-to-book (P/B), EV/EBITDA, PEG and interest coverage, are not on the page and not covered here. They are useful for specific sectors (P/B for banks, EV/EBITDA for capital-intensive businesses) and for comparing companies with different capital structures.


7.3.2 Quality of Earnings
EPS is accounting profit, and accounting profit can be managed. A company can report a rising EPS by booking revenues early, delaying expenses, or capitalizing costs that should be expensed. To know whether the company is actually generating value, you must check the quality of those earnings against the cash the company generates.
The game provides Free Cash Flow (FCF) and Earnings per Share (EPS), but not Cash Flow from Operations. The most direct quality check available is therefore the FCF-to-EPS ratio:
\[
\text{Earnings Quality} = \frac{\text{FCF per share}}{\text{EPS}}
\]
A ratio near 1.0 means the company is generating enough free cash to back its reported profit. A ratio persistently below 1.0 (e.g., 0.4 or 0.6) is a red flag: the company is reporting earnings on paper but not generating the cash to back them up. This usually means it is spending heavily just to maintain its asset base (high capital expenditure), or it is not collecting its receivables. A ratio above 1.0 means the company is generating more cash than it reports in profit, which is generally a sign of conservative accounting.
Three checks tell you if the earnings are real:

FCF-to-EPS. The most direct test of whether reported profit is “real.” If FCF per share is persistently lower than EPS, the earnings are of low quality. Track the ratio over the years the page shows: a ratio that is improving is a better signal than a ratio that is high but falling.
ROI and ROE trends. A rising ROE might just mean the company is taking on more debt (since equity is the denominator). Check whether ROI, the return on all capital invested, moves in the same direction. If ROI is falling while ROE is rising, the profitability is an artifact of leverage, not a genuine improvement in the business. A healthy company shows both ROE and ROI rising together, or ROI rising faster than ROE.
EPS growth stability. Is the EPS growth steady, or jumping around? Stable growth is higher quality than volatile growth.



7.3.3 Solvency and Liquidity
Two ratios on the page describe the balance sheet, what the company owns and what it owes, and tell you if it can survive a bad year:

Current Ratio. Current assets divided by current liabilities. This measures whether the company has enough short-term assets to cover its short-term bills. A ratio below 1.0 is a warning sign: the company cannot pay what it owes in the next twelve months. A ratio rising from below 1.0 to above 1.0 is a strong sign of improving liquidity.
Debt-to-Equity (D/E). Total debt divided by shareholders’ equity. A high D/E means the company is highly leveraged. A falling D/E means it is paying down debt or growing equity, which reduces risk.



7.3.4 Relative Valuation
An absolute price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio tells you almost nothing. A P/E of 10 might be expensive for a slow-growing utility but cheap for a fast-growing tech company. You have to compare it to two benchmarks:

Its own history. Compare the current P/E to the company’s five-year average P/E. If the current P/E is much higher than its historical average, the stock is more expensive than it used to be. The market has re-rated it.
The market. Compare the current P/E to the market average. If the stock’s P/E is higher than the market, it is trading at a premium.







TipApplying the numbers: a worked example



Suppose you are looking at a European energy company (the numbers are invented). You read the page in three steps:

Quality of Earnings. EPS has grown from €1.20 to €4.00 over four years, which is strong. ROI is 16 %, comfortably above the cost of capital. Most importantly, FCF per share has turned from negative (−€0.40) to positive (€3.00). The FCF-to-EPS ratio is therefore \(3.00 / 4.00 = 0.75\): the company is generating 75 cents of free cash for every euro of reported profit. It is not a perfect 1.0, but the trend is strongly positive (the ratio was negative four years ago), and 0.75 is high enough to confirm the earnings are backed by cash.
Solvency and Liquidity. The current ratio has risen from 0.9 to 1.6. It is now comfortably above 1.0. D/E has fallen from 57 % to 31 %. The company has deleveraged and improved its short-term liquidity.
Relative Valuation. The current P/E is 12. The five-year average P/E is 6.5. The market average is, say, 15.

Versus history: \(12 / 6.5 \approx 1.85\). The stock is almost twice as expensive as its own history.
Versus market: \(12 / 15 = 0.8\). The stock is cheaper than the market.


The verdict. The fundamentals are clearly better than they were four years ago. The FCF-to-EPS ratio confirms the profit is real and backed by cash, the current ratio confirms the company can pay its bills, and the D/E confirms it is deleveraging. However, the stock has re-rated from a P/E of 6.5 to a P/E of 12. While it still trades below the broad market, it is nearly double its historical multiple. The market has already priced in the recovery. The thesis is “strong, high-quality fundamentals, but the valuation premium relative to its own history leaves no margin of safety.” That supports a neutral or underweight position, not because the company is weak, but because the price is full.

8.1 Fees
With the allocation set, the fund needs a fee: it pays the firm’s staff and earns its profit.
The fee of each fund is set on the Clients page, in percent a year, and charged per round (a quarter-round charges a quarter of it). Three facts from the game:
A workable rule for the first rounds: a modest fee, differentiated by type (higher for the dynamic funds), unchanged until the results show how AuM responds. Fees are the one decision the game lets you revise every round with an immediate, visible effect in Projections; changing them every round, however, makes the attribution of AuM changes to your investment decisions impossible.

title: 8  Fees, projections, submission
text:
Higher fees turn clients away and raise revenue per client.
Clients tolerate a fee better when their risk-adjusted return is good.
Dynamic clients respond to marketing and accept higher fees; conservative clients want fees low and transparent.

Does each fund’s projected tracking error match what station 4 said, roughly?
Does any fund show cash that you did not intend (a filter leaving a segment unmatched, Chapter 7)?

title: 9  Reading the results
text:
9.1 Micro attribution: diagnosing the source of the active return
After the deadline, the Results page shows how each fund did in the round just completed: fund performance before and after fees, AuM and flows, satisfaction, the firm’s financials, and the ranking against the other teams in the universe.
For more detail, the Analyst page shows the performance ratios, factor coefficients, and performance attribution. The strategic allocation analysis compares your strategic allocation with the optimal allocation for the client.
Read the page in this order. Start with the ratios: the active return and the information ratio tell you whether the tactical tilt worked. Then read the attribution to see which decision was responsible. Then read the strategic allocation analysis, which tells you whether the γ estimate is right. The first two are adjustments you make every round; the third is an adjustment you make once.
The Analyst page has three attribution tabs: Active return, Allocation, and Selection. Allocation is the effect of how much you put in each segment (the tactical tilt); Selection is the effect of which assets you held inside each segment (the security selection). Together they decompose the active return by source, so you can see which decision (currency, asset class, industry, maturity, factor) was responsible for the outcome. This is micro attribution.

title: 9  Reading the results
text:
9.1.1 The three questions micro attribution answers
When the IR is negative, the first question is always: which decision went wrong? The attribution tabs answer three questions, in order:

Was it the allocation or the selection? The Allocation tab shows the effect of where you were positioned (the tactical tilt). The Selection tab shows the effect of what you held (the security selection). If the allocation effect is negative and the selection effect is zero, the tactical tilt was wrong. If the allocation effect is zero and the selection effect is negative, the security selection was wrong. If both are negative, both were wrong.
Was it the currency or the asset class? Within each tab, the breakdown by Currency and Asset class tells you whether the problem was a currency bet (e.g., overweight euro when the euro fell) or an asset-class bet (e.g., overweight equities when equities fell). If the currency effect is large and the asset-class effect is small, the problem was the currency.
Was it the industry, the maturity, or the factor? If the currency and asset-class effects are small but the industry, maturity, or factor effects are large, the problem was at the security level. This is where the security selection shows up. A large negative industry effect means the fund was overweight an industry that underperformed; a large negative factor effect means the fund was tilted toward a factor that underperformed (e.g., value when growth was winning).



9.1.2 A worked example: diagnosing a negative IR
Suppose the Orange fund has an active return of −0.8 % in a round, and so a negative IR. The Analyst page shows:



Tab
Category
Effect




Allocation
Currency
−0.5 %


Allocation
Asset class
−0.1 %


Selection
Industry
−0.2 %


Selection
Factor
0.0 %



The diagnosis. The total active return is −0.8 % (the sum of the effects). The allocation effect is −0.6 % (currency −0.5 % + asset class −0.1 %), which is the larger part. Within the allocation, the currency effect is the dominant term. The selection effect is −0.2 %, all from industry. The factor effect is zero.
What this tells you. The problem was primarily a currency bet that went wrong, not the asset-class allocation and not the security selection. The tactical tilt was in the wrong currency; the industry selection was a secondary problem; the factor tilt was neutral.
What to do next round. The currency bet is the first thing to fix. Go back to the view that produced the currency tilt (Chapter 5) and ask whether the view was wrong or the currency movement was a surprise. If the view was wrong, lower its confidence or drop it. If the currency movement was a surprise, the view may have been right but the outcome was unlucky; keep the view but check whether the tracking-error budget was large enough to accommodate the surprise.
The industry selection is a secondary problem. It is a smaller effect, and it may be an artifact of the value-weighting rule rather than a deliberate security selection. If the fund is on automatic allocation, do not try to fix it; if it is on manual allocation, review the industry overweights.
The factor tilt is neutral. Do not change it.


9.1.3 What micro attribution cannot tell you
Micro attribution is a diagnostic tool, not a decision tool. It tells you where the active return came from, but it does not tell you whether the decision was right in expectation. A currency bet that lost money this round may have been the right bet given the information at the time. The attribution tells you the outcome; the record of the views tells you whether the outcome was consistent with the process.
The rule of thumb: change the decision only if the attribution shows a systematic problem, not a one-off loss. A currency bet that lost money once is a draw. A currency bet that has lost money three rounds in a row is a systematic error, and the attribution tells you to fix it. This is the same principle as the IR: one round is not evidence of skill, and one round is not evidence of failure either.


9.1.4 The connection to the performance ratios
The micro attribution and the performance ratios are two sides of the same coin. The ratios tell you whether the fund added value; the attribution tells you where it came from. Read them together:

A negative IR with a large currency effect means the currency bets were wrong.
A negative IR with a large asset-class effect means the tactical tilt was wrong.
A negative IR with a large industry or factor effect means the security selection was wrong.
A positive IR with a large allocation effect means the tactical tilt was right.
A positive IR with a large selection effect means the security selection was right.

The ratios give you the verdict; the attribution gives you the reason. Use both.

title: 9  Reading the results
text:
9.2 Defining the performance ratios
The game reports four ratios per fund. They measure different things, and a fund can look good on one and bad on another.

9.2.1 Sharpe ratio
Excess return per unit of total volatility:
\[
\text{Sharpe} = \frac{R_p - R_f}{\sigma_p}
\]
It penalises both upside and downside volatility, so a fund that swings wildly in both directions scores lower than one that swings only upward.


9.2.2 Sortino ratio
Excess return per unit of downside volatility:
\[
\text{Sortino} = \frac{R_p - R_f}{\sigma_{\text{downside}}}
\]
It does not penalise upside volatility, so a fund with large gains and small losses scores much higher on Sortino than on Sharpe. Useful when the client cares more about losses than gains.


9.2.3 Treynor ratio
Excess return per unit of market risk:
\[
\text{Treynor} = \frac{R_p - R_f}{\beta_p}
\]
It isolates systematic risk, which makes it useful for funds held as part of a diversified portfolio. Note: if the fund’s beta is negative, the Treynor is negative even when the return is positive. Read it alongside the beta.


9.2.4 Information ratio
Active return per unit of active risk (tracking error):
\[
\text{IR} = \frac{\text{Active Return}}{\text{Tracking Error}}
\]
It is the ratio that matters for the tactical tilt, because it measures the skill of the active decisions, not the return of the fund as a whole.






WarningBefore or after fees



The game’s information ratio compares the fund’s return after fees with the benchmark’s return before fees. A fund that charges a fee therefore shows a negative information ratio whenever its tilt earned less than the fee, even if the tilt added return. To judge the tilt, compare the fund’s return before fees with the benchmark’s. The rules in this chapter refer to that comparison.

title: 9  Reading the results
text:
9.3 Reading the factor coefficients
The game reports five coefficients per fund, from a four-factor model. They tell you what kind of risk the fund is taking.

Alpha: return not explained by the factors. Positive is good.
Market beta: sensitivity to the market. Negative means the fund hedges against downturns.
HML beta: value (positive) vs. growth (negative).
MOM beta: momentum (positive) vs. contrarian (negative).
RMW beta: quality (positive) vs. junk (negative).

A fund with positive alpha, HML, MOM and RMW is a value-momentum-quality fund with skilled management. A fund with negative alpha and RMW but high MOM is a momentum-junk fund with poor management.

title: 9  Reading the results
text:
9.4 Reading the strategic allocation analysis
The lower half of the Analyst page compares your strategic allocation with the allocation the game’s parameters hold as optimal for the client, and gives a recommendation. The recommendation compares your weight to the target range for that segment, which is the range consistent with the client’s γ. A weight outside the range means the γ estimate or the reading of a rule is off.

“Balanced allocation.” Your weight is inside the target range. No change.
“Overweighted.” Your weight is above the range.
“Underweighted.” Your weight is below the range.

The direction tells you which way to adjust γ. Overweighted in equities means your γ is too low; move it up. Overweighted in government bonds means your γ is too high; move it down.

title: 9  Reading the results
section: 9.5 Actionable takeaways: what to do with the numbers
text:
9.5 Actionable takeaways: what to do with the numbers
The ratios and the attribution tell you what happened. To decide what to do next round, you need to translate them into actions. This section says how.

9.5.1 If the information ratio is below 0
What it means: The active return was negative relative to the risk taken. The tactical views were wrong, or the tracking-error budget was too large for the quality of the views.
What to do: Reduce the size of the tactical tilts. Either use fewer views, lower the confidence on the views you have, or narrow the maximum deviation band in station 4. If the IR is negative for three rounds in a row with high confidence, stop entering that view entirely.


9.5.2 If the information ratio is between 0 and 0.5
What it means: The active return was positive, but modest relative to the risk taken. The views were slightly right, or the tracking-error budget was too loose.
What to do: Keep the views, but check whether the confidence levels are calibrated. If views you entered with high confidence keep producing a small IR, lower the confidence next round.


9.5.3 If the information ratio is above 0.5
What it means: The views were right relative to the risk taken. The tactical process is working.
What to do: Keep doing what you are doing. Do not increase the tracking-error budget just because the IR is high; the budget is there to protect the client, not to maximise the score.


9.5.4 If the Sharpe ratio is high but the information ratio is low (or zero)
What it means: The fund generated good absolute risk-adjusted returns, but the tactical decisions did not add value. The high Sharpe comes from the strategic allocation, not from the tactical tilts.
What to do: Check the attribution. If the selection effect is zero and the allocation effect is zero, the tactical allocation is identical to the strategic allocation. That is fine if you had no views, but if you entered views and the IR is zero, the views were neutralised by the model (e.g., because the confidence was too low). Raise the confidence or do not enter the view.


9.5.5 If the Sortino ratio is much higher than the Sharpe ratio
What it means: The fund’s volatility is skewed to the upside. The fund has large positive returns and small negative ones.
What to do: Nothing. This is a good outcome. The client is getting upside volatility without the corresponding downside, which is exactly what a risk-averse client wants.


9.5.6 If the Sortino ratio is much lower than the Sharpe ratio
What it means: The fund’s volatility is skewed to the downside. The fund has large negative returns and small positive ones.
What to do: Check the attribution for a large negative allocation effect. If the fund is taking concentrated positions that have gone wrong, pull them back. The client’s loss aversion makes downside volatility particularly costly.


9.5.7 If the alpha is positive but the IR is negative
What it means: The fund is generating excess return relative to the factor model (good management), but the tactical allocation is underperforming the benchmark (bad tactical decisions). The two are unrelated: alpha is measured against factors, IR is measured against the benchmark.
What to do: Fix the tactical views, not the strategic allocation. The strategic allocation is generating alpha; the tactical tilts are destroying value.


9.5.8 If the market beta is negative
What it means: The fund moves opposite to the market. It is a hedge.
What to do: Check whether this is intended. If the client is risk-averse and the fund is holding defensive assets, a negative beta is fine. If the client is growth-oriented and the fund is hedging unintentionally, reduce the defensive weight.


9.5.9 If the strategic allocation analysis says “Overweighted”
What it means: The fund is holding more of a segment than the optimal allocation for the client’s γ.
What to do: If the overweight is in equities, raise the γ estimate (the client is more risk-averse than you thought). If the overweight is in bonds, lower the γ estimate. Change γ once, early, and record why.


9.5.10 If the satisfaction is falling but the IR is positive
What it means: The fund is beating the benchmark, but the client is unhappy. The most likely cause is that the fund is too far from the guidance bands (the client wants a specific allocation, not just a good return), or the fee is too high.
What to do: Compare the fund’s weights to the guidance bands. If the fund is outside the bands, pull it back. If the fund is inside the bands, check the fee.

title: 9  Reading the results
text:
9.6 Satisfaction and AuM
Satisfaction moves with three things: the distance to the optimal allocation, the risk the fund took against what the client expects, and the fee. AuM follows satisfaction and risk-adjusted performance with a lag.

title: 9  Reading the results
text:
9.7 Feeding it back
For the next round, in this order:

Pull back any extreme position.
Revise the γ estimate if the strategic allocation analysis says so, once.
Revise the confidence of the views that were wrong; add new views from the new outlook.
Revisit the fee only if AuM moved for no investment reason.

Then Chapter 5 again.

title: 9  Reading the results
text:
9.8 Deliverable of this step
A short written review per fund in the team forum: attribution by effect, verdict on each view, distance to the optimal allocation and what you conclude for γ, satisfaction and AuM, the decision for the next round.

title: Appendix A — The allocation app
text:
A.1 What it is
A Shiny app, provided with the course, that runs the allocation method of this book on the course dataset. It has four stations that follow Chapters 3 to 6. It does not connect to the game; you read numbers off it and type them into the game’s grids.
Source and installation: the course repository (2024_CESIM_Invest). It needs R with the packages shiny, DT, xts and quadprog; start it with shiny::runApp() in the app folder, or use the hosted instance your instructor names.

title: Appendix A — The allocation app
text:
A.2 The data

data/classes_monthly.csv: the 21 positions, monthly total returns in US dollars, unhedged, with an index series; the full history the course uses. The strategic benchmark is defined on the 16 positions without the money market; the app’s default selection leaves the five money-market positions out, and they can be added for analysis.
data/riskfree_monthly.csv: the US money-market rate, monthly.
data/cap_shares.csv: the capitalisation shares of the five equity markets, for the home rule.

Positions are named <region>_<class>: US_money_market, UK_government, EU_credit, CH_equity, JP_equity, GLOBAL_commodity. Excess returns are total returns minus the money-market rate of the same month. Annualisation: mean × 12, covariance × 12.

title: Appendix A — The allocation app
text:
A.3 Station 1 · Strategic Asset Analysis
Inputs: the positions (default the 16 benchmark positions), the part of the sample in percent of the observations (default all). Outputs: annualised statistics (excess return, volatility, Sharpe ratio, skewness, worst calendar year, maximum drawdown), the correlation matrix, the growth of 100.

title: Appendix A — The allocation app
text:
A.4 Station 2 · Strategic Asset Allocation
Inputs: γ (whole numbers), home market and home share, objective (quadratic utility, minimum variance, maximum Sharpe), a label; floors and caps by asset class, by currency and per position. The problem solved:
\[
\max_w \; \mu' w - \frac{\gamma}{2}\, w' \Sigma w
\quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum w = 1,\; w \ge 0,\; \text{floors and caps},\; \text{home rule},
\]
with the home rule as one linear equality per foreign equity market: \(w_x = (1-h)\, s_x
\sum_{\text{equity}} w\), where \(h\) is the home share and \(s_x\) the capitalisation share of market \(x\) outside the home market. Solved with quadprog::solve.QP(D = \gamma\Sigma, d = \mu, A, b, meq). Minimum variance sets μ = 0; maximum Sharpe is the best point of a sweep over γ. Weights are rounded to half a percent, the residual into the home equity position.
Outputs: the allocation as a currency × asset class matrix with sums, the positions with raw and rounded weights, class and currency totals, in-sample results of the fixed weights rebalanced monthly (expected excess return, volatility, Sharpe, best and worst calendar year, maximum drawdown), the binding limits, the in-sample path, the efficient frontier under the same limits, the constraint rows, and R code that reproduces the run. Fix this allocation as an SAA hands it to stations 3 and 4; several SAAs can be fixed, by label.

title: Appendix A — The allocation app
text:
A.5 Station 3 · Tactical Analysis
Inputs: τ (default 0.05) and the views, typed one per line: US_equity 12 50 is an absolute view (US equities earn 12 % a year over cash, confidence 50 %); EU_equity > CH_equity 2 60 is a relative view (euro-area equities beat Swiss equities by 2 points a year, confidence 60 %). The confidence is optional and defaults to 50; lines starting with # are ignored; a list of position names is in the panel. The views apply to every fixed SAA; a selector chooses which SAA’s prior and posterior the table shows.
Prior: \(\Pi = \gamma \Sigma w_{\text{SAA}}\) (reverse optimisation with the SAA’s own γ and the unrounded weights). Posterior (He and Litterman 1999):
\[
\mu_{BL} = \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} + P'\Omega^{-1}P\right]^{-1}
          \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1}\Pi + P'\Omega^{-1}Q\right],
\qquad
\Sigma_{BL} = \Sigma + \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} + P'\Omega^{-1}P\right]^{-1},
\]
with \(\Omega\) diagonal and \(\Omega_k = \frac{1-c_k}{c_k}\,\tau\, p_k'\Sigma p_k\), so that c = 1/2 is the He–Litterman setting. Outputs: per position the SAA weight, the sample mean, the prior, the posterior and the change; the views as parsed.

title: Appendix A — The allocation app
text:
A.6 Station 4 · Tactical Asset Allocation
Inputs: the maximum deviation per position (band, default 0.05) and the tracking-error budget (default 2 % a year, 0 = none). One press computes the tactical allocation of every fixed SAA under the same views. For each SAA, the problem of station 2 on \((\mu_{BL}, \Sigma)\) with that SAA’s γ and limits but without the home rule, plus \(w_{\text{SAA}} - d \le w \le w_{\text{SAA}} + d\). The home rule is left out because it defines the benchmark; kept, a view on one equity market could not act. The sample covariance Σ is used, not \(\Sigma_{BL}\): \(\Sigma_{BL}\) raises the measured risk by about \((1+\tau)\) as soon as any view is entered and moves weight from equities into bonds for no reason of the views. If a budget is set and the tracking error \(\sqrt{(w - w_{\text{SAA}})'\Sigma(w - w_{\text{SAA}})}\) exceeds it, the deviation is scaled to the budget. Outputs: a summary table with the tilt by asset class, tracking error and active return per fund, and a tab per fund with the SAA, TAA and deviation matrices, the active-position figures and the binding limits. A negative expected active return is flagged in both. Without views the TAA equals the SAA, and a view that agrees with the prior leaves it there.

title: Appendix A — The allocation app
text:
A.7 Saving your work
Station 2 saves the fixed SAAs (their inputs and weights), the views and the tactical settings as a JSON file and loads such a file back. On loading, the SAAs are recomputed from their inputs on the current data, so a loaded file is always consistent with the dataset in use. Save the file in the team forum; it is the team’s record of the funds and views.

title: Appendix A — The allocation app
text:
A.8 Tests
tests/check_recipe.R confirms that the app’s constraint builder and solver reproduce a hand-written quadratic programme for twenty client cases; tests/check_taa.R confirms that the tactical allocation equals the strategic one without views and under a view that agrees with the prior, that a negative view on one equity market lowers that market, and shows one view at work with a tracking-error budget.

title: Appendix B — Proposed changes to the app and the game
text:
B.1 Simplifications of the flow
Planning only. Nothing here is implemented; each item names what it would simplify in the flow of Chapters 2 to 9 and what it would take.
Station 0: the client. A form with the two decisions (σ and μ of each portfolio, taken or turned down) and the rules; the app computes the γ bracket, shows it, and carries the rules into station 2 as the limits. Removes the hand calculation of Chapter 2 and the manual entry of floors. Small.
Band check. Load the client’s guidance bands (from the course’s allocation workbook) and flag, in station 2 and station 4, any class outside its band. Removes the manual check of Chapters 4 and 6. Small; needs the bands in a machine-readable file in the app’s data/.
Game-format export. A button that writes the strategic or tactical matrix in the exact layout of the game’s grid (currency × asset class, percent) to the clipboard or a CSV. Removes typing errors. Small.
Outlook import. A paste field for the analyst’s segment estimates of the round (yields, spreads, expected excess market return, factor premia per currency) and a rule that turns them into candidate views against the prior, with the confidence derived from the expected range. Chapter 5 by hand becomes one paste. Medium; needs the game’s export format for the outlook.
All funds at once. Run stations 2 to 4 for the firm’s up to four funds in one pass: one views panel, a tab per fund, one combined export. Station 4’s “same views for every fixed SAA” table is the first step. Medium.
Round log. Keep, per fund and round, the SAA, the views, the TAA, the tracking error, and after the round the realised return and attribution (from the Results Excel), so that Chapter 9’s “judge the views” is a table rather than memory. Medium; needs the Results Excel format.

B.2 Extensions that implement further decisions
Security selection (Chapter 7). From the tactical segment weights to positions: value or equal weighting, an ESG floor, and the tracking error of the resulting stock book against the segment line; optionally overweights by factor loading or industry with their contribution to tracking error. Needs asset-level returns and ratings in the app’s data (ratings as levels, which the course dataset does not carry yet). Large.
Performance attribution (Chapter 9). Brinson–Fachler on the game’s Results Excel: allocation, selection and currency effects against the fixed SAA, per round and cumulative. Medium; the inputs are the round’s segment returns and weights.
Tracking-error optimisation proper. Replace the scaling of station 4 by an optimisation with the tracking error as a constraint (a second-order cone, or a search over the active risk aversion), so that the TAA at a budget is optimal rather than a shrunk optimum. Small to medium.
Estimation risk as a discussion tool. A toggle in station 2 that shows what shrinkage of the means toward the grand mean (or a Kan–Zhou-type combination) would do to the allocation, next to the plain optimum. Not for the benchmark, which stays the plain optimum; for the discussion of why a plain optimum is fragile and why the game defines the benchmark this way. Small.
Currency hedging as a hypothetical. Show what the allocation would be if foreign bonds could be hedged (local excess returns plus the interest differential, local covariance), next to the unhedged one the game allows. Makes Chapter 3’s point visible. Small; the hedged series would have to be added to the course dataset.

B.3 Suggestions for the game itself
Client texts and guidance bands. The October 2026 client profiles and guidance bands replace the current ones.
Strategic allocation analysis on the Analyst page. It compares the fund’s strategic allocation with the optimal allocation held in the game’s parameters. If it reports the distance exactly, a team can iterate to the hidden allocation round by round; a coarse report (inside the guidance band / outside, or a distance rounded to five points) keeps the client-reading exercise alive.
Tracking error on the Investment strategy page. It is estimated from the game’s own forecasts and a short history; the app’s figure uses the full history. Stating the horizon and the data behind the game’s estimate would make the two comparable.
Exports. A CSV export of the Economic outlook’s segment estimates and of the Results attribution would make the outlook import and the round log above possible.
